description: We are a team of four with diverse backgrounds and a shared passion for creating. Beyza specializes in test automation, Emre is an emergency physician passionate about coding, Oğuz Kağan is a sixth-grade content creator who discovered programming through Scratch, and Ayşe is a fourth-year Computer Engineering student with a keen interest in design. Ready, Martian? is our first project together, born at the NASA Space Apps Challenge. This is just the beginning!
summary:
Ready, Martian? is a browser game that puts kids aged 7–12 in charge of a small outpost in Gale Crater on Mars. Over an 11-sol mission, players manage the outpost's resources and make the kinds of decisions a real crew would face, sol by sol. The game is built on real NASA data about Gale Crater, so the conditions players respond to come from the real Mars, not an imaginary one. Everything leads up to a dust storm on the final sol, and how well the outpost holds up depends on the choices players made along the way.

We built it for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge because kids learn science best when they get to act on it. Instead of memorizing facts about Mars, players discover for themselves why planning, resource management and careful decision-making matter on a mission. The game is playable in any browser on itch.io with no installation, so it works at home or in a classroom. Our goal is to spark curiosity about space exploration and help kids picture themselves as future astronauts.
details:
Ready, Martian? is a browser game in which children aged 7–12 keep four astronauts alive in Gale Crater, Mars, for 11 sols (Mars days). Every sol uses the weather NASA's Curiosity rover actually measured there in May 2024, the real solar flares and storms recorded in NASA's DONKI database, and the real Earth–Mars light delay. The mission ends with the solar particle storm of 20 May 2024, the largest radiation surge Curiosity has measured.

How it works: each sol has four short steps. (1) Briefing: a story chapter, a base map whose colored pins show what needs care, the real weather and space weather news. (2) Energy: the player shares the day's solar power, computed from the real Sun angle, atmospheric dust and panel soiling, between life support, heating, the greenhouse and the antenna, with live previews of tonight's oxygen, water, temperature and battery. (3) Crew jobs: each of the four astronauts (roles from NASA's CHAPEA Mars analog) gets one of nine jobs, such as repairing the oxygen generator, cleaning solar panels, tending lettuce, radioing Mission Control or carrying water bags to the radiation shelter. (4) Night: timed alarm cards. Asking Earth for help costs the real 16-minute light-time round trip.

What makes it creative: skipped jobs come back sols later as delayed consequences, such as a solar panel that cracks unseen, clogged CO2 filters or wilting crops, so children learn why real crews keep up routine maintenance. During the final storm, each astronaut's radiation dose depends on where they are working when the alarm sounds.

Benefits and impact: the game teaches life support, power budgeting, radiation shielding, food production and communication delay through visible cause and effect rather than long text. Every number links to its NASA source, and cards are labelled "Real data" or "Game event". An Explorer view is for children and an Engineer view, with formulas and constants, is for teachers. Five badges reward a healthy crew, no shortages, storm safety, a harvest and a science discovery.

Tools: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no server. The simulation is separate from the interface and is checked by an automated balance test that plays seven strategies, plus a browser test that clicks through all 11 sols on phone and laptop screen sizes. The whole game, including data and 39 illustrations, is a single 1.7 MB HTML file that works offline on school computers, with keyboard, mouse or touch. The props were sketched in Sumo Paint and then generated with Google Gemini; Claude (Anthropic) assisted with the code, data processing and documents.

Factors considered: ages 7–12 (pictures first, one color code, short science notes, optional hints), real data accuracy (any rule that is not a measurement is labelled as an assumption), accessibility (reduced-motion support, screens from 390 px phones to laptops) and classroom use without internet.
